decks.title: Animal Kingdom — Part 1: Basis of classification and the non-chordate phyla
goals: Classify animals by levels of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation and notochord
Describe the salient features of the ten non-chordate phyla with examples
Place an animal in its phylum from a set of features

slides.heading: Animal Kingdom
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how animals are sorted, then the ten phyla without a notochord.

visual.alt: Flow of the animal kingdom into non-chordates and chordates

slides.narration: More than a million kinds of animals have been described. To study them, biologists look for fundamental features shared by groups: how the body is organised, its symmetry, its layers and body cavity, and whether it has a notochord. These features sort animals into phyla.

slides.heading: Levels of organisation
slides.body_md: All animals are multicellular eukaryotes, but their cells are organised differently: **cellular, cell-tissue, organ and organ-system** levels.

rows: Cells loosely arranged; little division of labour
Cells of one function arranged in tissues

visual.alt: Table of levels of organisation with the phyla that show each

slides.narration: In sponges the cells are loosely arranged and do separate jobs without forming tissues. In coelenterates, cells doing the same job form tissues. Flatworms have organs made of tissues. Roundworms and all higher animals have organs working together in organ systems, such as digestive and circulatory systems.

slides.heading: Symmetry
slides.body_md: **Asymmetrical** (sponges), **radial** (coelenterates, ctenophores, adult echinoderms) and **bilateral** (annelids, arthropods and most others).

slides.narration: A sponge cannot be cut into equal halves in any plane. A radially symmetrical animal, such as a sea anemone, can be cut into equal halves by any plane through its central axis. A bilaterally symmetrical animal, such as an earthworm, has right and left halves that mirror each other along one plane only.

slides.heading: Diploblastic and triploblastic animals
slides.body_md: In the embryo, **diploblastic** animals have two germ layers, ectoderm and endoderm, with an undifferentiated **mesoglea** between. **Triploblastic** animals have a third layer, the **mesoderm**, between them.

rows: Body not built from germ layers
Ectoderm and endoderm, with an undifferentiated mesoglea between

visual.alt: Table of germ layers in sponges, diploblastic and triploblastic animals

slides.narration: Ectoderm forms the outside of the body and endoderm lines the gut. Coelenterates and ctenophores have only these two layers with a jelly-like mesoglea between them. All animals from flatworms upwards also have mesoderm, which gives rise to muscles and many organs.

slides.heading: Body cavity: coelom
slides.body_md: A **coelom** is a body cavity **lined by mesoderm**. **Coelomates** have one, **pseudocoelomates** have mesoderm only as scattered pouches between ectoderm and endoderm, and **acoelomates** have none.

slides.narration: In flatworms, mesoderm fills the space and there is no cavity. In roundworms there is a cavity, but mesoderm lies only in scattered pouches, so it is a pseudocoelom. In annelids, arthropods, molluscs, echinoderms, hemichordates and chordates, the cavity is lined by mesoderm all round: a true coelom.

slides.heading: Segmentation, notochord and gut
slides.body_md: **Metamerism:** body divided into segments with serial repetition of some organs (earthworm). **Notochord:** a mesodermal rod on the dorsal side in the embryo of **chordates**. **Gut:** **incomplete** (one opening) or **complete** (mouth and anus).

visual.alt: Table of segmentation, notochord, gut and circulation in animal groups

slides.narration: An earthworm is divided into segments, each repeating some organs. Chordates have a rod, the notochord, along the back at some stage. A flatworm has a gut with one opening, while a roundworm has a complete gut with a mouth and an anus. Blood circulation may be open or closed.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: naming the phylum from features
slides.body_md: Name the phylum of each animal. P: coelomate, segmented body with jointed appendages. Q: radial, two germ layers, stinging cells on tentacles. R: bilateral, round in cross-section, mesoderm only in scattered pouches.
bullets: **P:** coelomate and segmented gives Annelida or Arthropoda; jointed appendages point to **Arthropoda**.
**Q:** diploblastic gives Coelenterata or Ctenophora; stinging cells (cnidoblasts) point to **Coelenterata**.
**R:** a pseudocoelom gives **Aschelminthes**.

visual.alt: Worked table placing three animals in Arthropoda, Coelenterata and Aschelminthes

slides.narration: Narrow the list step by step. Coelomate and segmented leaves annelids and arthropods, and jointed appendages choose arthropods. Two germ layers leaves coelenterates and ctenophores, and stinging cells choose coelenterates. A pseudocoelom belongs only to roundworms.

slides.heading: Porifera: the sponges
slides.body_md: Mostly marine, **asymmetrical**, cellular level. **Water canal system:** water enters through **ostia** into the **spongocoel**, lined by **choanocytes**, and leaves through the **osculum**. Skeleton of **spicules** or **spongin** fibres. Hermaphrodite.

slides.narration: Chordates have a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, gill slits in the pharynx, a ventral heart and a post-anal tail. Non-chordates lack the notochord and gill slits, have a ventral solid double nerve cord, a dorsal heart if one is present, and no post-anal tail.

slides.heading: Three subphyla
slides.body_md: **Urochordata** and **Cephalochordata** are called **protochordates**. In vertebrates the notochord is replaced by a **vertebral column** and the heart is two-, three- or four-chambered.

slides.narration: In tunicates such as Ascidia, the notochord is present only in the larval tail. In Branchiostoma, the lancelet, the notochord runs from head to tail throughout life. notes.title: Animal Kingdom — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Basis of classification
sections.body_md:
Animals are multicellular, eukaryotic and heterotrophic. Biologists group them using fundamental features that are shared within a group.

**Levels of organisation.** In **sponges** the cells are loosely arranged and show a **cellular** level of organisation, with little division of labour. In **coelenterates** and **ctenophores** cells doing the same function are arranged into tissues: the **cell-tissue (tissue) level**. In **flatworms** tissues are grouped into **organs**. In **aschelminthes** and all higher phyla the organs work together as **organ systems**.

**Symmetry.** Sponges are **asymmetrical**. **Radial symmetry**, in which any plane passing through the central axis divides the body into two equal halves, is found in coelenterates, ctenophores and adult echinoderms. **Bilateral symmetry**, with right and left halves along one plane only, is found in annelids, arthropods and other higher animals.

**Germ layers.** **Diploblastic** animals have two embryonic layers: an external **ectoderm** and an internal **endoderm**, with an undifferentiated layer, the **mesoglea**, between them (coelenterates, ctenophores). **Triploblastic** animals have a third layer, the **mesoderm**, between ectoderm and endoderm (platyhelminthes to chordates).

**Coelom.** The body cavity **lined by mesoderm** is the **coelom**. Animals with a true coelom are **coelomates** (annelids, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms, hemichordates, chordates). In **pseudocoelomates** (aschelminthes) the mesoderm is present only as scattered pouches between the ectoderm and the endoderm, so the cavity is not fully lined. Animals with no cavity, such as flatworms, are **acoelomates**.

**Segmentation.** In **metamerism**, the body is externally and internally divided into segments with serial repetition of at least some organs, as in earthworms (annelids and arthropods).

**Notochord.** A mesodermally derived rod-like structure formed on the dorsal side during embryonic development in some animals. Animals with a notochord are **chordates**; those without are **non-chordates**.

**Other features.** The digestive system may be **incomplete** (a single opening serves as mouth and anus) or **complete** (a separate mouth and anus). Circulation may be **open** (blood pumped into open body cavities, as in arthropods and molluscs) or **closed** (blood always in vessels, as in annelids and chordates).

sections.body_md:
**Porifera (sponges).** Mostly marine, a few freshwater; asymmetrical; cellular level. Pores called **ostia**, a central cavity (**spongocoel**) and an opening, the **osculum**, form a **water canal system** that carries water for food gathering, respiratory exchange and removal of wastes; the spongocoel and canals are lined by **choanocytes** (collar cells). The skeleton is made of **spicules** or **spongin** fibres. Sponges are **hermaphrodite** (eggs and sperms are formed by the same individual); fertilisation is internal and development is indirect, through a larva. They also reproduce asexually by fragmentation. Examples: *Sycon*, *Spongilla*, *Euspongia*.

**Coelenterata (Cnidaria).** Aquatic, mostly marine; radial symmetry; tissue level; diploblastic. A central **gastrovascular cavity** has a single opening, the **hypostome**. **Cnidoblasts** (cnidocytes), with stinging capsules (nematocysts) on the tentacles and body, serve for anchorage, defence and capture of prey. Two body forms: the sessile, cylindrical **polyp** (*Hydra*, *Adamsia*) and the free-swimming, umbrella-shaped **medusa** (*Aurelia*). Those with both forms show **metagenesis** (alternation of generations): in *Obelia* polyps produce medusae asexually and medusae form polyps sexually. Corals have a calcium carbonate skeleton. Examples: *Physalia*, *Adamsia*, *Pennatula*, *Gorgonia*, *Meandrina*.

**Ctenophora (sea walnuts or comb jellies).** Exclusively marine, radial, diploblastic, tissue level. Eight external rows of ciliated **comb plates** help locomotion; digestion is both extracellular and intracellular; **bioluminescence** is well marked. Sexes are not separate; reproduction is only sexual with external fertilisation and indirect development. Examples: *Pleurobrachia*, *Ctenoplana*.

**Platyhelminthes (flatworms).** Dorsoventrally flattened; bilateral; triploblastic; **acoelomate**; organ level. Mostly endoparasites with **hooks and suckers**; some absorb nutrients through the body surface. **Flame cells** help in osmoregulation and excretion. Sexes are not separate; fertilisation is internal; development goes through many larval stages; high regeneration capacity (*Planaria*). Examples: *Taenia* (tapeworm), *Fasciola* (liver fluke).

**Aschelminthes (roundworms).** Circular in cross-section; bilateral; triploblastic; **pseudocoelomate**; organ-system level; free-living or parasitic. The alimentary canal is complete with a muscular pharynx; an excretory tube removes wastes through the excretory pore. Sexes are separate (dioecious), females often longer than males; fertilisation is internal; development is direct or indirect. Examples: *Ascaris*, *Wuchereria* (filarial worm), *Ancylostoma* (hookworm).

**Annelida.** Marine, freshwater or terrestrial; bilateral; triploblastic; **metamerically segmented**; **coelomate**; organ-system level. Longitudinal and circular muscles help locomotion; *Nereis* has lateral appendages, **parapodia**, for swimming. **Nephridia** serve for osmoregulation and excretion; circulation is **closed**; the nervous system has paired ganglia joined to a double ventral nerve cord. *Nereis* is dioecious; earthworms and leeches are monoecious. Examples: *Nereis*, *Pheretima* (earthworm), *Hirudinaria* (leech).

**Arthropoda.** The **largest phylum**: over two-thirds of all named species are arthropods. Organ-system level; bilateral; triploblastic; segmented; coelomate. A **chitinous exoskeleton** covers a body of head, thorax and abdomen with **jointed appendages**. Respiratory organs: gills, book gills, book lungs or the tracheal system. Circulation is **open**. Sense organs: antennae, compound and simple eyes, statocysts. Excretion by **Malpighian tubules**. Mostly dioecious, internal fertilisation, mostly oviparous, direct or indirect development. Examples: *Apis*, *Bombyx*, *Laccifer* (economically important); *Anopheles*, *Culex*, *Aedes* (vectors); *Locusta* (gregarious pest); *Limulus* (king crab, a living fossil).

**Mollusca.** The second largest phylum. A **calcareous shell** covers an unsegmented body with a distinct head, a muscular **foot** and a visceral hump; the skin forms a **mantle** enclosing the **mantle cavity** with feather-like **gills** (respiratory and excretory); the mouth has a rasping **radula**. Usually dioecious and oviparous with indirect development. Examples: *Pila*, *Pinctada* (pearl oyster), *Sepia*, *Loligo*, *Octopus*, *Aplysia*, *Dentalium*, *Chaetopleura*.

**Echinodermata.** Marine; **spiny-skinned**, with an endoskeleton of **calcareous ossicles**. Adults are **radially symmetrical**, larvae bilateral; triploblastic; coelomate; the digestive system is complete. The distinctive **water vascular system** helps in locomotion, capture and transport of food, and respiration; an excretory system is absent. Sexes separate; fertilisation usually external; indirect development with a free-swimming larva. Examples: *Asterias*, *Echinus*, *Antedon*, *Cucumaria*, *Ophiura*.

**Hemichordata.** Once a subphylum of Chordata, now a separate non-chordate phylum. Worm-like marine animals with a body of **proboscis, collar and trunk**; open circulation; respiration by gills; excretion by the proboscis gland; sexes separate; external fertilisation; indirect development. Examples: *Balanoglossus*, *Saccoglossus*.

sections.heading: 3. Chordates up to classes
sections.body_md:
**Phylum Chordata.** Chordates are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and coelomate with organ-system level of organisation. They have a **notochord**, a **dorsal hollow nerve cord**, **paired pharyngeal gill slits**, a **post-anal tail** and a **closed circulatory system** with a ventral heart (present at some stage of life). In non-chordates the central nervous system is ventral, solid and double, there is no notochord or gill slits, the heart (if any) is dorsal, and the post-anal tail is absent.

**Subphyla.** **Urochordata** (notochord only in the larval tail: *Ascidia*, *Salpa*, *Doliolum*) and **Cephalochordata** (notochord from head to tail throughout life: *Branchiostoma*, the lancelet) are the **protochordates**. In **Vertebrata** the notochord is replaced by a **cartilaginous or bony vertebral column** in the adult; there is a muscular ventral heart with two, three or four chambers, kidneys for excretion and osmoregulation, and paired appendages (fins or limbs). Vertebrates are divided into **Agnatha** (jawless) and **Gnathostomata** (jawed; **Pisces** and **Tetrapoda**).

**Cyclostomata.** Ectoparasites on some fishes; elongated body with **6–15 pairs of gill slits**; sucking, circular mouth without jaws; cartilaginous cranium and vertebral column; limbless. Marine, but they migrate to fresh water to spawn and die soon after; the larvae return to the ocean. Examples: *Petromyzon* (lamprey), *Myxine* (hagfish).

**Chondrichthyes.** Marine, streamlined, **cartilaginous endoskeleton**; mouth ventral; notochord persists throughout life; **separate gill slits without an operculum**; skin tough with **placoid scales**; teeth are modified placoid scales; powerful jaws; predaceous. **No air bladder**, so they must swim constantly to avoid sinking. **Two-chambered heart**; cold-blooded. Some have electric organs (*Torpedo*) or a poison sting (*Trygon*). Sexes separate; males have **claspers** on the pelvic fins; **internal fertilisation**; mostly viviparous. Examples: *Scoliodon*, *Pristis*, *Carcharodon*, *Trygon*.

**Osteichthyes.** Marine and freshwater; **bony endoskeleton**; streamlined; mouth mostly terminal; **four pairs of gills covered by an operculum**; skin with **cycloid or ctenoid scales**; an **air bladder** regulates buoyancy; **two-chambered heart**; cold-blooded; sexes separate; fertilisation usually external; oviparous; direct development. Examples: *Exocoetus* (flying fish), *Hippocampus* (sea horse), *Labeo* (rohu), *Catla*, *Clarias* (magur), *Betta*, *Pterophyllum*.

**Amphibia.** Live in water and on land; two pairs of limbs; **moist skin without scales**; eyes with eyelids; **tympanum** as the ear; the alimentary canal, urinary and reproductive tracts open into a **cloaca**; respiration by gills, lungs and skin; **three-chambered heart** (two atria, one ventricle); cold-blooded; fertilisation external; oviparous; direct or indirect development. Examples: *Bufo*, *Rana*, *Hyla*, *Salamandra*, *Ichthyophis* (limbless).

**Reptilia.** Creeping or crawling; **dry, cornified skin with epidermal scales or scutes**; tympanum as the ear; two pairs of limbs when present; heart usually **three-chambered, four-chambered in crocodiles**; cold-blooded; snakes and lizards shed their scales as skin cast; fertilisation internal; oviparous; direct development. Examples: *Chelone* (turtle), *Testudo*, *Chameleon*, *Calotes*, *Crocodilus*, *Alligator*, *Hemidactylus*, *Naja* (cobra), *Bangarus* (krait), *Vipera*.

**Aves.** **Feathers**; forelimbs modified into **wings** (flightless: ostrich); hind limbs with scales for walking, swimming or perching; dry skin with an oil gland at the base of the tail; **fully ossified endoskeleton with hollow (pneumatic) long bones**; **crop and gizzard** in the digestive tract; **four-chambered heart**; **warm-blooded**; lungs with air sacs; internal fertilisation; oviparous; direct development. Examples: *Corvus*, *Columba*, *Psittacula*, *Struthio*, *Pavo*, *Aptenodytes* (penguin), *Neophron*.

**Mammalia.** Found in many habitats; the most unique feature is the **mammary glands** that nourish the young; **hair** on the skin; **external ears (pinnae)**; different types of teeth; **four-chambered heart**; **warm-blooded**; lungs; internal fertilisation; mostly viviparous with direct development. Examples: *Ornithorhynchus* (platypus, oviparous), *Macropus*, *Pteropus*, *Camelus*, *Macaca*, *Rattus*, *Canis*, *Felis*, *Elephas*, *Equus*, *Delphinus*, *Balaenoptera*, *Panthera*.

*Counting rule used in questions:* the chambers of the heart are two in fishes, three in amphibians and most reptiles, and four in crocodiles, birds and mammals.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling flatworms pseudocoelomate (they are acoelomate; roundworms are pseudocoelomate).
- Writing that all echinoderms are radial (adults are radial, larvae bilateral).
- Saying coelenterates have a mouth and an anus (the gut has a single opening).
- Putting the heart of a crocodile with the three-chambered reptiles (it is four-chambered).
- Placing whales or dolphins with fishes (they are mammals).
- Forgetting that cartilaginous fishes have no air bladder and no operculum.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a distinguishing feature of a phylum or class; an example; the heart chambers; a term such as metamerism.
- 2–3-mark answers: radial versus bilateral symmetry; diploblastic versus triploblastic; types of coelom with examples; salient features of one phylum; cartilaginous versus bony fishes.
- 5-mark answers: classification basis; non-chordate phyla compared; chordate features and subphyla; classes of vertebrates compared.
- Counting items: tallies from a table of animals, gill slits from pairs, total chambers — show the working.

questions.stem_md: Explain the basis of classification of animals under levels of organisation, symmetry, germ layers and body cavity, naming a phylum for each category.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Levels of organisation.** Sponges (Porifera) have a cellular level, with cells loosely arranged; coelenterates have a cell-tissue level; flatworms have an organ level; roundworms and higher phyla have organ systems.

**Symmetry.** Sponges are asymmetrical; coelenterates, ctenophores and adult echinoderms are radially symmetrical, so any plane through the axis gives equal halves; annelids and arthropods are bilaterally symmetrical, with one plane giving mirror halves.

**Germ layers.** Coelenterates are diploblastic, with ectoderm and endoderm and a mesoglea between; flatworms and all higher animals are triploblastic, with a mesoderm as well.

**Body cavity.** Flatworms are acoelomate; roundworms are pseudocoelomate, with scattered mesodermal pouches; annelids, arthropods, molluscs, echinoderms, hemichordates and chordates are coelomate, the cavity being lined by mesoderm.

Segmentation (annelids, arthropods) and the notochord (chordates) also separate groups.

questions.stem_md: A bath sponge is dried and its soft fibrous skeleton is used for bathing. This skeleton is made of
questions.solution_md: Sponges have a skeleton of spicules or spongin fibres; the bath sponge Euspongia has a soft spongin skeleton — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which structures on the tentacles of a coelenterate help in anchorage, defence and the capture of prey?
questions.solution_md: Cnidoblasts (cnidocytes) with stinging capsules serve these functions — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An animal found floating near the surface has an umbrella-shaped body and trailing tentacles and swims freely. It is the
questions.solution_md: The free-swimming, umbrella-shaped body is the medusa (as in Aurelia); the sessile cylindrical form is the polyp — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In Obelia, which statement about its two body forms is correct?

options.text_md: Polyps form medusae asexually and medusae form polyps sexually
Polyps form medusae sexually and medusae form polyps asexually
Only the polyp reproduces, by budding, and no medusa forms

questions.solution_md: Obelia shows metagenesis: polyps produce medusae asexually and medusae form polyps sexually — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A marine diver sees a transparent animal that glows in the dark and swims by beating eight rows of ciliated plates. It belongs to
questions.solution_md: Eight rows of ciliated comb plates and bioluminescence mark the ctenophores (comb jellies) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A flattened parasitic worm from the intestine of a cow has hooks and suckers. In such worms, the flame cells help in
questions.solution_md: Flame cells of flatworms (Platyhelminthes) help in osmoregulation and excretion — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A planarian cut across its body regrows each piece into a whole worm. This ability, high in flatworms, is called
questions.solution_md: Flatworms such as Planaria have a high capacity for regeneration — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about a roundworm such as Ascaris is correct?

options.text_md: It is hermaphrodite and has flame cells.
The sexes are separate and the female is often longer than the male.
It has an incomplete gut with only a mouth.
It is segmented and has nephridia.

questions.solution_md: Aschelminthes are dioecious, the females often being longer than the males, with a complete gut — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A marine sandworm such as Nereis swims with the help of lateral appendages. These are called
questions.solution_md: Aquatic annelids such as Nereis have lateral appendages, parapodia, that help swimming — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The organs that carry out osmoregulation and excretion in an earthworm are
questions.solution_md: Annelids have nephridia; arthropods use Malpighian tubules, flatworms flame cells and hemichordates the proboscis gland — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A museum curator notes that two-thirds of the named species in her insect collection share a chitinous exoskeleton and jointed appendages. Excretion in these animals is mainly by
questions.solution_md: Arthropods excrete mainly through Malpighian tubules — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A scorpion, a crab and a grasshopper all breathe differently. Which list names respiratory organs found in arthropods?

options.text_md: Gills, book gills, book lungs and the tracheal system
Lungs, air sacs, gills and skin
Water vascular system, tube feet and gills

questions.solution_md: Arthropods breathe by gills, book gills, book lungs or tracheae — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A health officer is planning to control Anopheles, Culex and Aedes, which spread diseases. To which phylum do these animals belong, and what is a feature they share with it?
questions.solution_md: Mosquitoes are arthropods, with a chitinous exoskeleton and jointed appendages — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The king crab Limulus, called a living fossil, is a member of
questions.solution_md: Limulus is an arthropod and is a living fossil — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A garden snail scrapes soft algae from a stone with a file-like organ in its mouth. This organ is the
questions.solution_md: Molluscs have a rasping, file-like radula for feeding — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A pearl oyster (Pinctada), a cuttlefish (Sepia) and an octopus all have

options.text_md: a body of many identical segments with parapodia
a soft unsegmented body with a mantle covering the visceral hump
a spiny skin with calcareous ossicles
a post-anal tail and a notochord

questions.solution_md: These are molluscs: soft, unsegmented body with a head, foot, visceral hump and mantle — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A starfish creeps over a rock and pulls open a mussel. The system chiefly responsible for its movement and food capture is the
questions.solution_md: Echinoderms have a water vascular system for locomotion, capture and transport of food, and respiration — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A marine biologist notes that the free-swimming larva of a sea urchin is bilaterally symmetrical, whereas the adult is not. What does this show about adult echinoderms?

options.text_md: They are radially symmetrical, though their larvae are bilateral
They are asymmetrical like sponges in all stages
They are bilateral in the adult and radial as larvae
They are radially symmetrical in all stages of life

questions.solution_md: Adult echinoderms are radially symmetrical but the larvae are bilaterally symmetrical — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A worm-like marine animal has a body divided into proboscis, collar and trunk, and breathes through gills. It is a member of
questions.solution_md: Proboscis, collar and trunk mark the hemichordates (Balanoglossus, Saccoglossus) — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The free-swimming larvae of echinoderms are radially symmetrical.

**Reason (R):** Adult echinoderms are radially symmetrical.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: the larvae are bilaterally symmetrical. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A coelenterate has a gut with a single opening, the hypostome, which acts as both mouth and anus.
questions.solution_md: True. The gastrovascular cavity opens by a single opening, so the gut is incomplete.

questions.stem_md: The file-like rasping organ in the mouth of a mollusc, used in feeding, is called the ______.
questions.solution_md: Radula.

questions.stem_md: The alternation of the polyp and medusa forms in Obelia is called ______.
questions.solution_md: Metagenesis.

questions.stem_md: Match each animal (column I) with its phylum (column II).
questions.solution_md: Sycon is a sponge, Pleurobrachia a comb jelly, Taenia a flatworm and Asterias a starfish.

questions.stem_md: A ctenophore has 8 rows of comb plates, and each row carries 24 plates in an imagined specimen. How many comb plates does the animal have in all?
questions.solution_md: $8 \times 24 = 192$ comb plates.

questions.stem_md: A museum has 90 named animal species. If exactly two-thirds of them are arthropods, how many species are arthropods?
questions.solution_md: $90 \times \dfrac{2}{3} = 60$ species.

questions.stem_md: An earthworm has 120 body segments. A student cuts it after segment 40, counting from the head end. How many segments are in the posterior piece?
questions.solution_md: $120 - 40 = 80$ segments.

questions.stem_md: Describe the path of water through a sponge and state two functions of this flow.

answer.model_answer_md: Water enters through the **ostia**, passes into the central cavity, the **spongocoel**, lined by **choanocytes**, and leaves through the **osculum**. The flow brings **food** and **oxygen** (respiratory exchange) and carries away **wastes**.

questions.solution_md: Ostia, spongocoel, osculum; two functions.

questions.stem_md: A swimmer is stung by a jellyfish. Name the cells responsible, where they are found and one use of them to the jellyfish.

answer.model_answer_md: The **cnidoblasts** (cnidocytes), which contain **stinging capsules**, are found on the **tentacles and body** of coelenterates. They serve for **defence**, **capture of prey** and **anchorage**.

questions.solution_md: Cnidoblasts on tentacles; defence, prey, anchorage.

marking_scheme.step: Cnidoblasts with stinging capsules on tentacles and body

questions.stem_md: Name the larger group of worms to which a liver fluke belongs and state two features that adapt it to a parasitic life.

answer.model_answer_md: A liver fluke is a **flatworm (Platyhelminthes)**. Parasitic forms have **hooks and suckers** for holding on to the host, and some **absorb nutrients directly through the body surface** from the host.

questions.solution_md: Platyhelminthes; hooks and suckers; absorption.

marking_scheme.step: Absorption of nutrients through the body surface

questions.stem_md: State two features of ctenophores that distinguish them from coelenterates.

answer.model_answer_md: Ctenophores have **eight external rows of ciliated comb plates** for locomotion, which coelenterates lack. They are exclusively **marine** and show well-marked **bioluminescence**, and reproduce **only sexually**, whereas coelenterates have cnidoblasts and polyp and medusa forms.

questions.solution_md: Comb plates; bioluminescence; only sexual reproduction.

questions.stem_md: Give three differences between flatworms and roundworms.

answer.model_answer_md: **Flatworms** are **dorsoventrally flattened**, **acoelomate** and have an **organ** level with an **incomplete gut**; many are parasites with hooks and suckers and have **flame cells**. **Roundworms** are **circular in cross-section**, **pseudocoelomate**, with an **organ-system** level and a **complete gut**; their **sexes are separate**.

questions.solution_md: Shape, body cavity, gut.

questions.stem_md: List three salient features of phylum Annelida, with two examples.

answer.model_answer_md: Annelids are **bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and coelomate** animals living in marine, freshwater or terrestrial habitats, with a **metamerically segmented** body at the **organ-system** level. They have **longitudinal and circular muscles** for locomotion, **nephridia** for excretion and osmoregulation, and a **closed circulatory system**. Examples are **Nereis**, with parapodia, and the **earthworm Pheretima**.

questions.solution_md: Segmentation, coelom, nephridia, closed circulation; examples.

questions.stem_md: Why is Arthropoda called the largest phylum of the animal kingdom? State two features of its members.

answer.model_answer_md: Over **two-thirds of all named species** on Earth are arthropods, which makes it the **largest phylum**. Their body is covered by a **chitinous exoskeleton** and divided into **head, thorax and abdomen**, with **jointed appendages**; they have an **open circulatory system** and excrete through **Malpighian tubules**.

questions.solution_md: Two-thirds of named species; two features.

questions.stem_md: A student examines a pond snail. Name its three main body regions and describe the mantle cavity and the radula.

answer.model_answer_md: A mollusc has a distinct **head**, a muscular **foot** and a **visceral hump**, covered by a **calcareous shell**. The soft skin forms a **mantle** over the hump, enclosing the **mantle cavity** with feather-like **gills** that serve respiration and excretion. In the mouth the **radula** is a file-like organ for feeding.

questions.solution_md: Head, foot, visceral hump; mantle cavity with gills; radula.

questions.stem_md: State three features of echinoderms, and explain what is peculiar about their symmetry.

answer.model_answer_md: Echinoderms are marine, have a **spiny skin** with an endoskeleton of **calcareous ossicles**, and a **water vascular system** that helps in locomotion, food capture and respiration; they have no excretory system. **Adults are radially symmetrical but the larvae are bilaterally symmetrical.**

questions.solution_md: Spines, ossicles, water vascular system; radial adult, bilateral larva.

questions.stem_md: Describe the salient features of Porifera, Coelenterata and Ctenophora, with two examples each.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Porifera.** Mostly marine, asymmetrical, with a cellular level of organisation. Water enters through ostia into the spongocoel, lined by choanocytes, and leaves through the osculum, bringing food and oxygen and removing wastes. The skeleton is of spicules or spongin; they are hermaphrodite. Examples: *Sycon*, *Spongilla*.

**Coelenterata.** Aquatic, mostly marine, radially symmetrical, tissue level, diploblastic. A gastrovascular cavity has one opening, the hypostome. Cnidoblasts on the tentacles serve for anchorage, defence and prey capture. The body forms are polyp and medusa, with metagenesis in *Obelia*. Examples: *Physalia*, *Adamsia*.

**Ctenophora.** Exclusively marine, radial, diploblastic, with eight rows of ciliated comb plates and well-marked bioluminescence; reproduction is only sexual. Examples: *Pleurobrachia*, *Ctenoplana*.

questions.solution_md: Salient features and examples of three phyla.

questions.stem_md: Compare Platyhelminthes, Aschelminthes and Annelida in body cavity, symmetry, level of organisation, special structures and examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Platyhelminthes.** Dorsoventrally flattened, bilateral, triploblastic, acoelomate, organ level. Mostly endoparasites with hooks and suckers; flame cells for osmoregulation and excretion; high regeneration. Examples: *Taenia*, *Fasciola*.

**Aschelminthes.** Circular in cross-section, bilateral, triploblastic, pseudocoelomate, organ-system level. The gut is complete with a muscular pharynx; sexes are separate, females often longer. Examples: *Ascaris*, *Wuchereria*, *Ancylostoma*.

**Annelida.** Bilateral, triploblastic, coelomate and metamerically segmented, organ-system level. They have longitudinal and circular muscles, nephridia, a closed circulation and, in *Nereis*, parapodia. Examples: *Nereis*, *Pheretima*, *Hirudinaria*.

So the body cavity changes from none, to a pseudocoelom, to a true coelom, and segmentation first appears in the annelids.

questions.solution_md: Three worm phyla compared.

questions.stem_md: Describe the salient features of Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata and Hemichordata, with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Arthropoda.** The largest phylum, with over two-thirds of named species. Triploblastic, coelomate, bilateral and segmented, with a chitinous exoskeleton, head, thorax and abdomen, jointed appendages, open circulation and Malpighian tubules. Respiration is by gills, book gills, book lungs or tracheae. Examples: *Apis*, *Bombyx*, *Anopheles*, *Locusta*, *Limulus*.

**Mollusca.** A calcareous shell, an unsegmented soft body with head, muscular foot and visceral hump; a mantle cavity with gills; a radula. Examples: *Pila*, *Pinctada*, *Sepia*, *Octopus*.

**Echinodermata.** Marine, spiny-skinned with calcareous ossicles, radial adults and bilateral larvae, water vascular system, no excretory system. Examples: *Asterias*, *Echinus*, *Cucumaria*.

**Hemichordata.** Worm-like marine animals with proboscis, collar and trunk, open circulation and gills. Examples: *Balanoglossus*, *Saccoglossus*.

questions.solution_md: Four phyla with examples.

questions.stem_md: A rock-pool survey records five unknown animals: P is radial and diploblastic with stinging cells; Q has a calcareous shell, a muscular foot and a radula; R is segmented and coelomate with jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton; S has spiny skin and a water vascular system; T is a flat, acoelomate parasite with hooks. Name the phylum of each animal with reasons, and say which two share the coelomate condition but differ in segmentation.

answer.model_answer_md:
**P** is a **coelenterate**: radial symmetry, two germ layers and cnidoblasts. **Q** is a **mollusc**: shell, muscular foot and radula, with an unsegmented soft body. **R** is an **arthropod**: segmented coelomate with jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton. **S** is an **echinoderm**: spiny skin and a water vascular system. **T** is a **platyhelminth** (flatworm): acoelomate, flat, with hooks and suckers.

Q and R are both coelomates, but the mollusc is unsegmented while the arthropod is metamerically segmented. S is also coelomate and unsegmented. Segmentation, body cavity and special structures together fix each phylum.

questions.solution_md: Five phyla placed with reasons; coelomate comparison.

questions.stem_md: Mention two features of cyclostomes and explain their breeding habit.

questions.stem_md: Compare cartilaginous fishes and bony fishes on skeleton, gill cover and air bladder.

questions.solution_md: Skin, heart and fertilisation contrasts.

questions.stem_md: Explain three adaptations of a bird for flight.

questions.stem_md: State three features that place an animal in class Mammalia, and name one oviparous mammal.

answer.model_answer_md: Mammals have **mammary glands** that nourish the young, **hair** on the skin and **external ears (pinnae)**, with different types of teeth, a **four-chambered heart** and a **warm-blooded** body, and they breathe by lungs. questions.stem_md: Describe the fundamental features of phylum Chordata, contrast it with the non-chordates, and describe its three subphyla.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Features.** Chordates are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and coelomate with organ systems. At some stage they have a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, paired pharyngeal gill slits and a post-anal tail, and a closed circulatory system with a ventral heart.

**Contrast.** In non-chordates the nerve cord is ventral, solid and double, there is no notochord or gill slits, the heart (if present) is dorsal and there is no post-anal tail.

**Subphyla.** In *Urochordata* (*Ascidia*, *Salpa*) the notochord is present only in the larval tail. In *Cephalochordata* (*Branchiostoma*) it extends from head to tail and persists throughout life. In *Vertebrata* the notochord is replaced by a cartilaginous or bony vertebral column in the adult; there is a muscular ventral heart of two, three or four chambers, kidneys for excretion and osmoregulation, and paired fins or limbs. Urochordates and cephalochordates are called protochordates.

questions.stem_md: Describe the salient features of the jawless and jawed fishes, comparing cyclostomes, cartilaginous fishes and bony fishes with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Cyclostomata** (jawless): ectoparasites on some fishes, with a sucking circular mouth without jaws and 6–15 pairs of gill slits, a cartilaginous cranium and vertebral column and no limbs; they migrate to fresh water to spawn. *Petromyzon*, *Myxine*.

**Chondrichthyes:** marine, streamlined, with a cartilaginous skeleton and a ventral mouth. Separate gill slits without an operculum; placoid scales; no air bladder, so they must swim constantly; two-chambered heart; cold-blooded; males have claspers; internal fertilisation, mostly viviparous. *Scoliodon*, *Trygon*, *Carcharodon*.

**Osteichthyes:** marine or freshwater, with a bony skeleton; four pairs of gills under an operculum; cycloid or ctenoid scales; an air bladder regulates buoyancy; two-chambered heart; cold-blooded; fertilisation usually external, oviparous. *Labeo*, *Catla*, *Exocoetus*, *Hippocampus*.

questions.solution_md: Three fish classes compared.

questions.stem_md: Compare the four tetrapod classes, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia, with respect to body covering, heart, body temperature, fertilisation and examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Amphibia:** moist skin without scales, a cloaca, a tympanum, respiration by gills, lungs and skin, a three-chambered heart, cold-blooded, external fertilisation, oviparous. *Rana*, *Bufo*.

**Reptilia:** dry cornified skin with scales or scutes, lungs, a heart that is usually three-chambered but four-chambered in crocodiles, cold-blooded, internal fertilisation, oviparous with direct development. *Calotes*, *Crocodilus*, *Naja*.

**Aves:** feathers, wings, pneumatic bones, crop and gizzard, a four-chambered heart, warm-blooded, lungs with air sacs, internal fertilisation, oviparous. *Columba*, *Struthio*.

**Mammalia:** hair, mammary glands, pinnae, different types of teeth, a four-chambered heart, warm-blooded, lungs, internal fertilisation, mostly viviparous. *Canis*, *Macropus*, *Ornithorhynchus* (oviparous).

questions.solution_md: Four tetrapod classes compared.

questions.stem_md: A student claims: "Whales and sharks are both fishes because they live in water and swim, and all warm-blooded animals are viviparous." Evaluate this claim using the characters of the classes of chordates.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Whales.** The claim is wrong about whales. A whale such as *Balaenoptera* has mammary glands, hair (at least in part), lungs for respiration and a four-chambered heart, and it is warm-blooded; it is a mammal. Living in water does not decide the class.

**Sharks.** A shark is a cartilaginous fish: it has a cartilaginous skeleton, placoid scales, gill slits without an operculum, a two-chambered heart, and it is cold-blooded. So the two animals are in different classes and have nothing in common except their habitat.

**Warm-blooded and viviparous.** Only birds and mammals are warm-blooded. Birds are oviparous, with direct development, so the second part is false. Among mammals most are viviparous, but the platypus *Ornithorhynchus* is oviparous.

**Judgement.** Both parts of the claim fail: whales are mammals, not fishes, and warm-blooded does not mean viviparous.
